name: Gender-neutral aesthetics / 'pretty boy' / softboy

lead: This aesthetic aims for soft, delicate, androgynous features in men instead of heavy masculine angularity.
People pursue it with skincare, hair, grooming, makeup and clothing.

paras: Followers emphasize smooth skin, eyes, lips and styled hair, and choose clothing and grooming that read as soft and polished.
Mostly styling choices; any procedures people pair with it carry their own risks.

chain: Prioritise skin, hair, lashes and grooming
Softer, more harmonious and polished features
angle.text: Followers use skincare, haircare, grooming, eye and lash care, makeup and styling to emphasise smooth skin and delicate features. It is a styling approach rather than a single product, and the same tools are available to anyone regardless of bone structure.

lead: Gender-neutral, "pretty boy" or softboy aesthetics describe a look built on soft, delicate or androgynous features in men: clear skin, expressive eyes and lashes, fuller lips, a gentler jawline and well-kept hair, rather than heavy, angular dimorphism. People pursue it through skincare, hair, grooming, eye and lash care, makeup, fashion and sometimes facial procedures, and it is an alternative route to looking attractive for those who do not aim for a "chad" build. Because most of its tools are cosmetic and stylistic, the look can be worked on by anyone regardless of bone structure. [1][2][3]

The look has long precedent in popular culture, from 1970s glam figures such as David Bowie and Marc Bolan to Prince and Boy George, and Japanese and Korean pop culture has treated androgynous looks as a positive attribute. [1] In Japan the ideal of the bishonen (beautiful youth) is central to manga, anime and idol culture and has roots reaching back centuries. [4] In South Korea the related kkonminam ("flower handsome man") image, used since the late 1990s, centres on attractive young men who invest in grooming, fashion and cosmetics. [5] In the West, the metrosexual of the 1990s and 2000s and the e-boy and softboy styles of the late 2010s carried related ideas into mainstream and internet fashion. [6][7]

On looksmax.org, "pretty boy" is a recurring archetype that members compare with "chad" and discuss in threads about hair, eyes, skin and style. [2][3] Thread titles show the community weighing it against other routes: whether to "pretty boy max", "chad max" or "dom max", whether a "robust pretty boy" is the best archetype, and how people are treated when they look like one. [8][9][10] The look is mainly a styling and grooming approach; no clinical research addresses it as such, though studies of how masculine and feminine faces are perceived are relevant background. [1][11]
infobox: Androgyny, softboy, pretty boy, bishonen, kkonminam (flower boy), metrosexual, e-boy [4][5][6][7]

paras: The aesthetic emphasises softness: clear skin, expressive eyes, fuller lips, styled hair and a less pronounced jaw. Practitioners adapt fashion and grooming to match, including jewelry, makeup and unisex clothing, which became mainstream in men's fashion in the West and Asia. [1]

In a looksmax.org thread asking what pretty-boy aesthetics are, replies listed hair, long eyelashes, skin and good style, with one also naming facial width-to-height ratio, a pointed chin and "doe eyes". [3] A multi-part "pretty boy guide" on the same forum begins with the eye area, covering lash growth and lifting, conditioning serums and light eyeliner for those whose look suits it; a reply suggested contacts and eyebrows as further eye-area topics. [2]

sections.h: How people use it to improve their looks
paras: Skin is the first lever: followers describe a smooth, even complexion as the base of the look, pursued with ordinary skincare routines. Hair is the second, and looksmax.org members run threads on the best pretty-boy hairstyle and on pretty boys with receding hair. [3][12][13] The eye area is a third, using lash conditioning, lash lifts, brow shaping and, for some, light eyeliner. [2]

Clothing and grooming are adjusted to read as soft and polished rather than rugged. Wikipedia's androgyny article notes jewelry, makeup and unisex clothing in men's fashion, and the e-boy style is described as layered oversized knits, chains, dangle earrings and curtained hair. [1][7]

Some practitioners combine the look with other appearance work. The looksmaxxing article on Wikipedia separates low-risk "softmaxxing" such as skincare, grooming, clothing and fitness from "hardmaxxing" such as surgery, and the pretty-boy approach as described on the forum sits mainly in the first group. [14][2]

Androgynous fashion appears across the twentieth century, from 1920s flappers and Marlene Dietrich to Yves Saint Laurent's 1966 tuxedo suit, Bowie's Ziggy Stardust in 1972, and 1980s figures such as Prince and Boy George. [1]

Wikipedia's article on androgyny traces earlier male precedents, including the macaronis of mid-18th-century Georgian England, wealthy young men known for large wigs and lavish fashion, and later Mick Jagger's white dress at the 1969 Hyde Park concert, Marc Bolan's glitter and satin on Top of the Pops in 1971, and the December 1983 and January 1984 Smash Hits and Newsweek covers showing Boy George and Annie Lennox in matching makeup. [1] It adds that men's catalogues of the 1990s featured jewellery, makeup and designer stubble. [1]

Bishonen ("beautiful youth") is a Japanese term for a young man of androgynous beauty, with an aesthetic described as central to shojo manga and anime, popular with girls and women, and embodied by many idols from the talent agency Johnny & Associates. [4] The page describes the term as emerging in the Meiji era and androgynous glam rock in the 1970s as boosting the look's popularity. [4]

Visual kei, a Japanese music subculture that emerged in the early 1980s and took its name from a 1989 X Japan album slogan, is built around elaborate costume, makeup and styling. Many performers use androgyny or cross-dressing drawing on the onnagata tradition, and Gackt is cited as a well-known example of a bishonen-style image. [15] In 2008 the term "herbivore men" became popular in Japan for young men distancing themselves from traditional masculinity, described by Masahiro Morioka as gentle and non-aggressive in romance. [16]

Kkonminam has been used since the late 1990s for attractive young men who focus on style, grooming and fashion, often including cosmetics. [5] Late-1990s advertising and dramas replaced tough male images with men with smooth, fair skin and silky hair, and the 2009 drama Boys Over Flowers is credited with encouraging many men to take their appearance more seriously. [5] Global K-pop fans use the "flower boy" label for Korean male idols. [5]

A Wikipedia account links the Korean ideal to the Hwarang, the elite 'flower youth' warriors of ancient Silla described in Chinese sources as androgynously handsome, and to Japanese manga, dramas and visual-kei bands that reached Korea informally before Japanese culture was officially legalised in 1998. [5] The article says the Korean version is often described as having more purity, innocence and politeness than the Japanese bishonen, and that gender and sexual orientation are generally unambiguous in it. [5] It also reports that after Boys Over Flowers (2009), more South Korean men began to wear cosmetics and preppy outfits in traditionally feminine colours and prints, and that analysts such as Yonsei University professor Kim Hyun Mee attribute part of the trend to Korean women's growing independence and selectiveness. [5]

Wikipedia's K-pop article quotes sociologist Ingyu Oh saying the genre favours thin, tall, feminine looks with cute expressions regardless of whether performers are male or female, and its photo captions note male groups with prominent eye makeup and styled hair. [17]

Journalist Mark Simpson coined 'metrosexual' in The Independent on 15 November 1994, a blend of 'metropolitan' and 'heterosexual' for a man meticulous about style, grooming and appearance; the advertising agency Euro RSCG adopted it for a 2003 marketing study, and The New York Times ran 'Metrosexuals Come Out' that year. [6]

Wikipedia reports that retail analysts measured men's share of their own apparel purchases rising from 25 percent in 1985 to 52 percent in 1998 and 69 percent in 2004, and that magazines such as Details and Men's Vogue targeted this audience. [6] The article notes related labels that followed, including ubersexual, spornosexual and lumbersexual, and a view from researcher Devon Powers that marketers borrowed the term from 1990s queer culture to encourage men to shop. [6] Some men, it says, objected to the label while wanting the freedom to care about their appearance. [6]

sections.h: Softboy and e-boy styles on social media
paras: Wikipedia's article on the e-girl and e-boy subculture says it emerged in the late 2010s and was popularised by TikTok in 2018 and 2019, blending emo, scene and mall-goth looks with Japanese and South Korean street fashion. It says e-boys adopted a "soft-boy" look emphasising sensitivity and vulnerability, which some commentators link to a shift in ideals of male attractiveness. [7]

The same article lists boys' style elements as oversized sweaters, band merchandise over striped long-sleeves, chain accessories, dangle earrings and curtained hair, with makeup used by both sexes. It reports that Vogue covered e-girl makeup in 2020 and that designers including Hedi Slimane for Celine and Ludovic de Saint Sernin drew on e-boy fashion. [7] It also records criticism: singer James Blake objected to the "sad boy" label's portrayal of mental illness. [7]

Wikipedia describes looksmaxxing as having emerged in incel and manosphere forums in the 2010s, with the PSL forums creating a rating scale whose top tiers use the "Chad" label, and with media coverage from 2023 onward in outlets such as the BBC and The Guardian. [14] The pretty-boy look is discussed within this vocabulary as an alternative archetype to the chad.

Forum threads show the debate: titles ask whether a robust pretty boy is the best archetype or the chad, whether female attention favours a robust pretty boy, and who on the forum had the best pretty-boy ascension. [18][9][10] Others ask "pretty boy or chad" and how people treat a "cutecel pretty boy". [19][8]

No study addresses the pretty-boy or softboy aesthetic as such. A 2021 paper by Neil Hester, Eric Hehman and Benedict Jones in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, described on Wikipedia, found that perceived femininity and masculinity contribute independently to facial impressions, so a face can be rated high on both, and that some facial features predicted impressions of trust, dominance, threat and attractiveness; the authors argued that treating the two as opposite ends of one dimension was oversimplified. [1]

Wikipedia's physical attractiveness article summarises findings on masculine and feminine male faces: women's preferences for masculine faces vary with the menstrual cycle, in one study women in the follicular phase chose masculine faces more often than others, and one study reported that once perceived health is accounted for, facial masculinity makes little difference to a man's attractiveness. [11] It also notes that average masculinity preference differed between countries in a study of 4,794 young women, and that women who see themselves as attractive are more likely to choose masculine faces. [11]
No studies found on the aesthetic itself. Related research on how masculine and feminine facial features are perceived is summarised above. [1][11]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org the pretty-boy look is discussed as a target that members optimise with skin, hair, lashes and styling, often set against the "chad" archetype. [2][3][9]

claims.claim: Skin, hair, lashes and style define the pretty-boy look
The eye area is the first priority for the look
A robust pretty boy is the most attractive archetype to women
Softer looks are a legitimate route to attractiveness, not a fallback
Femininity and masculinity are not opposites, so a face can be both
Men can care about grooming without it undermining masculinity

timeline.event: Macaronis, young men known for large wigs and lavish fashion, appear in Georgian England as an early male precedent. [1]
Yves Saint Laurent's tuxedo suit marks a milestone in androgynous fashion. [1]
David Bowie's Ziggy Stardust persona brings androgynous glam to wide audiences. [1]
Visual kei emerges in Japan's underground music scene. [15]
Mark Simpson coins 'metrosexual' in The Independent. [6]
Japanese culture is officially opened to South Korea; kkonminam imagery spreads in commercials and dramas in the late 1990s. [5]
Euro RSCG's marketing study and a New York Times feature spread the metrosexual idea. [6]
The term 'herbivore men' becomes popular in Japan. [16]
The drama Boys Over Flowers is credited with encouraging Korean men to take appearance more seriously. [5]
TikTok popularises the e-boy and softboy look. [7]
Hester, Hehman and Jones publish work on independent contributions of femininity and masculinity to facial impressions. [1]
